text: No battle took this ground.
A signature did.
On the twenty-sixth of September, 1833, federal commissioners called thousands of Potawatomi, Ojibwe, and Odawa to Chicago and pressed them to sign.
The talks dragged on for weeks.
Many of the chiefs refused to sell, and the men who finally marked the paper did not all speak for the people that paper would bind.
One document swept it away.
The Three Fires nations gave up about five million acres across Illinois and the Michigan Territory, this lakefront among them.

In return the government promised five million acres west of the Mississippi, a hundred thousand dollars in goods, fourteen thousand dollars in cash a year for twenty years, money for mills and farm tools, and seventy thousand dollars for schools.
The Potawatomi got three years to leave.
Witnesses recorded what the leaving looked like.
In August 1835, around five thousand Potawatomi gathered at the agency house for their last annuity payment.
About eight hundred men rose and danced through the streets of Chicago.
They had roached their hair and tied hawk and eagle feathers nearly to the ground.
They painted their faces red and black, the foreheads, cheeks, and noses ridged with curved stripes edged in points.
They moved from the council house west along the river.
They stopped before every house they passed, crossed the north branch, and were gone.
John Caton, a young lawyer who would later sit on the Illinois Supreme Court, watched and called it a war dance.
The dancers knew it as something else.
Caton himself wrote that they understood it as the last dance on their native soil, a kind of funeral for old associations and memories.
The funeral was for the living.
The removal had only begun.
